one_paragraph_summary: Panganiban uses a nine-question Q&A format to explain the contrasting Comelec 2nd Division and SET rulings on Sen. Grace Poe. Q1 (procedure): Poe will file her MR with the Comelec en banc Monday; David, denied at SET, is poised to go to the SC; all cases -- plus three others pending in Comelec's First Division -- will be consolidated at the SC for a final ruling; meanwhile Poe's name will be printed on the ballots as in Estrada's 2010 case. Q2 (SET justices at SC review): No, having judged below, they can no longer judge above. Q3 (5-4 vote reliability): Not unreliable at all -- many landmark cases have been decided by one vote, including Lambino v. Comelec (8-7, Oct 26, 2006) trashing the parliamentary-system people's initiative and the US Supreme Court's Bush v. Gore (5-4, Dec 12, 2000) halting the Florida recount and ushering in Bush's election. Q4 (Legarda asking electorate to decide legal issues): No -- Legarda quoted Frivaldo v. Comelec (June 26, 1996) at length: 'the question really boils down to a choice of ... how to interpret and apply laws relating to elections: literal or liberal, the letter or the spirit, the naked provision or the ultimate purpose, legal syllogism or substantial justice, in isolation of or in the context of social conditions, harshly against or gently in favor of the voters' choice. In applying election laws, it would be far better to err in favor of popular sovereignty than to be right in complex but little understood legalisms.' She chose the liberal way: in case of doubt involving popular sovereignty, interpret to enable the electorate to elect freely their chosen leader. Q5 (Duterte): If Duterte's alleged DQ rests only on a typographical error, he should be allowed to run under Frivaldo's substantial-justice principle -- this does not mean CJ approves his human rights shortcuts or habitual cussing; legal eligibility is different from electoral acceptability. Q6 (social justice for a non-poor Poe): Social justice equally favors the disabled, sick, abandoned (like foundlings), infirm, mentally retarded, disaster-stricken, and everyone economically, socially, politically, racially, and medically disadvantaged -- not only the impoverished. Q7 (Dura lex sed lex for foundlings?): Dura lex sed lex is a favorite expression of lawyers educated under the Analytical School who interpret verba legis; the better way is to look at the spirit, intent, and substance of the law -- lawyers should be social engineers who help build just societies, not mere automatons or legal technicians applying laws strictly without considering effects on society. Q8 (other natural-born offices): Yes, thousands -- Comelec commissioners, COA, CSC, CHR, ombudsman, most judicial/prosecutorial posts, bureau directorships, board examiners, scholarship grantees, and others too numerous to fit. Foundlings should not be denied entry to all these offices. Q9 (Poe's American period): That is a political, not legal, question better answered by the people via their ballots. Not every question can or should be decided by tribunals. Let Poe explain to the people, and if the majority accepts her explanation and votes her to office, so be it. This is the essence of democracy. Vox populi vox Dei.
